summary:
Alabama is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework. Federal passport and visa rules, entry screening, federal custody and detention policy, and federal healthcare and funding measures apply in Alabama as they do elsewhere in the country.

Facility rules are the first thing a trans visitor encounters. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map tabulates state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and records Alabama as enacting such bans in 2022 and 2024. The 2022 statute, House Bill 322, signed on 8 April 2022 as Act No. 2022-290, requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with the gender recorded on their birth certificate, and the state Board of Education codified that rule in September 2022. A March 2024 measure extends the restriction to university facilities. Senate Bill 79, signed in February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and authorises separate single-sex spaces where biology, privacy, safety or fairness are implicated.

The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, citing a bathroom ban carried by the state's 'Don't Say Gay' legislation that reaches college campuses.

Gender-affirming care for minors is a felony in Alabama. The Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act, Senate Bill 184, signed on 8 April 2022 and effective from 8 May 2022, makes it a Class C felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison for a medical provider to supply gender-affirming care, including puberty blockers, hormones or surgery, to anyone under 19. The Eleventh Circuit allowed enforcement on 21 August 2023, and the ban remains in force after the plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025. A trans visitor accompanying a minor, or seeking care for one, is exposed to that prohibition.

Identity documents are closed to most trans people. Alabama permits amendment of birth certificates and driver's licences to a person's current sex only with documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" together with a name change. A January 2021 federal ruling in Corbitt v. Taylor invalidated the surgery requirement, but the Eleventh Circuit reversed it and the requirement stands. On 20 September 2024 the same court ruled that refusal to issue accurate licences did not violate the federal constitution; rehearing was denied on 13 November 2024 and judgment entered on 10 December 2024. Most transgender people cannot obtain an accurate licence and must carry daily identification showing the wrong gender, which the ACLU describes as exposing them to a high risk of harassment and violence during ID checks.

No statewide law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment and bullying. Alabama also has no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare and no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees. A trans visitor has no statewide public-accommodations recourse.

Alabama's hate-crime statute, in force since 1994, covers offences motivated by race, colour, religion, national origin, ethnicity, or physical or mental disability. Gender identity is not covered. Attempts to add sexual orientation failed: House Bill 533 passed the House 46 to 41 in April 2009 but received no Senate vote before adjournment on 15 May 2009, and House Bills 413 in 2016 and 8 in 2017 also failed.

Partner recognition is settled statewide. Eight counties were still refusing all marriage licences in 2017, but the Legislature required recording of marriage certificates in May 2019 and every county began recording for all couples, including couples read as same-sex under birth-sex status, on 29 August 2019. The 1996 Executive Order Number 24, the 1998 statute at Alabama Code § 30-1-19 and the June 2006 constitutional Amendment 774 remain unenforceable.

Violence data for Alabama is incomplete. A July 2026 national analysis drawing on TGEU and Williams Institute data records a killing rate of trans women in Alabama of 3.8 per 100,000 per year, a figure the source itself describes as an undercount floor, calculated on a 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025. Alabama's general homicide rate does not appear in the source material, so the comparison that would show whether this exceeds background violence cannot be made, and the figure should not be read as a measure of severity on its own.
tangentialFactors:
Alabama's sports rules track the same birth-sex principle. House Bill 391, enacted in April 2021 after passing the House 74 to 19 with two abstentions and signed by Governor Kay Ivey, requires all K-12 athletes to compete in sports based on the gender listed on their birth certificate. From 1 July 2021 public schools must assign single-sex teams by "biological sex". House Bill 261, signed on 30 May 2023, bars college and university competition on a team differing from sex assigned at birth even after gender-affirming hormone therapy, except in co-ed sports.

The criminal law on sexual conduct no longer reaches the visitor's relationship. Alabama Senate Bill 320, passed by the House on 23 May 2019 and the Senate on 28 May 2019, repealed the ban on "deviate sexual intercourse" with effect from 1 September 2019. The age of consent is 16, with a within-two-years exception extended to same-sex contact in 2019.

Public opinion in the state runs against trans-inclusive policy. Statewide polling in 2025 places Alabama among the lowest-support states for transgender-inclusive nondiscrimination and access policies.
localsOnly:
Municipal protections are limited and local. Birmingham has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since September 2017, and Montevallo since April 2018. Huntsville, Tuscaloosa and Montgomery provide public-employment protections only.

Adoption by same-sex couples is permitted in Alabama, but the courts have a documented history of hostility. The Supreme Court of Alabama held in 2002 that homosexual conduct created a strong presumption of parental unfitness, describing it as "abhorrent, immoral, detestable". The Child Placing Agency Inclusion Act, signed by Governor Kay Ivey in May 2017, protects faith-based agencies that refuse placements on religious grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
The March 2024 measure on university bathroom use is recorded in the source inventory as a bill, while the equality map records a facility ban enacted in 2024. Its operative scope, the institutions it covers and whether it is being enforced are not sourced.

Alabama's general homicide rate is absent from the inventory, so the recorded killing rate for trans women cannot be set against background violence. The 428-victim base is a multi-year national dataset rather than an Alabama count.

Enforcement data for the 1994 hate-crime statute as applied to transgender victims is not sourced, and no figures on prosecutions or charging decisions are available.

Whether Senate Bill 79's authorisation of separate single-sex spaces has been applied beyond schools and universities, for instance to government buildings or public accommodations, is not established by the sources.

The care ban's litigation status after the plaintiffs withdrew on 1 May 2025 is unresolved in the inventory; no later appellate ruling is recorded.
